#4239. Big Walk Set to Miss Out on Indie Awards Over AI Code Controversy

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

In March 2027, we’ll be seeing the next iteration of the Independent Games Festival, a celebration and awards show highlighting some of the biggest achievements in the indie gaming sphere. As far as indie games this past year go, an obvious contender is House House’s Big Walk, a cozy exploration game that encourages groups of users to traverse a large island and solve various puzzles using only basic coordination and communication skills. Big Walk did very well for itself, and was part of the discussion for the IGF awards, but a recent disclosure has put a rather sizable damper on those hopes.

Yesterday, a coalition of judges and jurists for the IGF, represented by game journalist and developer Austin Walker, publicly announced their stance on games made with AI: specifically, after lengthy discussion, the judges decided to refrain from voting for any game that utilized AI in any capacity whatsoever. Walker and the judges’ statement, which was posted to his Bluesky account, didn’t specifically mention Big Walk or House House, but it seems it didn’t take long for onlookers to put the pieces together.

Following intense speculation, one of House House’s developers, Bruno Dias, confirmed on his own Bluesky account that, yes, Big Walk does have a small portion of AI-written code within it that was not originally disclosed to players, though it was disclosed to the IGF judges. As a result of this, there is a distinct chance that any awards Big Walk was previously under consideration for are now forfeit.

After overwhelmingly negative reviews from fans Creative Assembly has responded to the mistakes made in Total War: SHOGUN 2 Complete Edition.

Around the same time as the judges’ announcement and Dias’s Bluesky post, House House updated the official FAQ on its website with information about the usage of AI in Big Walk.

“In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs,” the FAQ reads, estimating that “well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.”

The FAQ also adds that this statement is not “an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal.”

“We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”

Activision has updated Call of Duty: Black Ops 6's Steam page to confirm some in-game content has been generated by AI.

In his Bluesky post, Dias offered clarification on several points in an effort to “combat misinformation.”

“While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly "consultative" use and not code gen or agents.”

In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.

He added that this disclosure prompted a lot of discussion within IGF’s internal forums, some of which Dias found disingenuous or dumb, but he has no intention of outing anyone for their opinions or discussing the matter further. He also noted that, at least as far as his understanding of it goes, Big Walk’s particular usage of AI is not in violation of Steam’s AI disclosure policies, which are slightly different from those used by IGF.

As has frequently been the case in the last couple of years, this particular late-stage disclosure hasn’t gone over great with players. While Big Walk’s overall rating on Steam still remains at Overwhelmingly Positive, at the time of writing, an outpouring of negative reviews have begun to crop up, each expressing disappointment that House House waited as long as it did after the game’s very successful release to disclose its AI usage.

This entire event is rather similar to what transpired with the Indie Game Awards last year, when Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 had its title of Game of the Year stripped after the developers admitted to a similarly small usage of AI in the game’s development.

The specter of generative AI usage isn’t just limited to the deluge of overtly vibe-coded slop that’s been flooding Steam and itch.io recently; even the smallest usage of AI, especially when it’s not disclosed from the jump, can feel extremely disingenuous to players, doubly so in the indie scene, which prides itself on from-scratch, creativity-first game development.

Supermarket Simulator, a new indie game on Steam that recently went viral, has been blasted for its potential use of AI imagery.

#4238. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.

#4237. Logitech's Game Day gives employees a day off to play video games

If you've been keeping up with gaming news in recent weeks, you've probably noticed growing speculation about the number of gamers planning to take time off work to binge-play GTA VI when it launches on November 19th.

And whilst there's no shortage of news outlets highlighting the potential economic downside of this mass gaming exodus, one particularly renowned gaming company is looking at the positives.

In recognition of the positive cognitive and professional benefits gaming can provide, Logitech International has announced Logi Game Day, a dedicated day off for its employees to play games. The initiative follows findings from the tech giant's recent Logitech Ctrl Tomorrow study, which revealed that 81% of gamers believe gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety and correlates with stronger day-to-day work performance.

Alongside the company-wide day off, Logitech G will also host a streaming event at its Americas headquarters in San Jose to celebrate the occasion. And, rather conveniently, it'll take place on November 19th. Isn't it nice how things work out?

A separate study conducted by Logitech also found that 98.8% of enterprise IT decision-maker (ITDM) respondents believe gaming skills translate directly into workplace capabilities, including strategic thinking, complex problem-solving and performing under pressure.

These findings prompted Logitech's chief executive officer, Hanneke Faber, to declare: "It's time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time. As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other."

Logitech G's general manager, Robin Piispanen, who'll be hosting the Logi Game Day event, also highlighted the team-building benefits of gaming: "Whether diving into a game like GTA VI or Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4, shaving seconds off lap times in Forza, or teaming up in an online battle, Game Day gives our team a shared purpose," he says. "We see firsthand how Logitech employees who sharpen their skills in-game translate directly back to work and problem-solving."

"Play is not the opposite of work," said Elaine Laird, Logitech's chief people officer. "When people have dedicated time to log off, decompress and immerse themselves in play, they return with clearer focus, renewed energy and fresh approaches to complex challenges."

While it would be somewhat premature to suggest that companies across every industry will eventually embrace similar initiatives, Logitech's decision does reflect a changing attitude towards the positive role gaming can play in our everyday lives. And, as the saying goes, great things have small beginnings.

So here’s hoping that when GTA VII rolls around somewhen in the 2040’s, we’ll all be enjoying a dedicated Game Day without having to call in sick!

#4236. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

Heartopia’s My Little Pony collaboration is close, and the pre-launch event has already kicked off.

Heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which launched a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

The Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

Badge Pull Tokens are your big reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

Heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

If any of that sounds interesting, definitely log in now to play the pre-launch event, which should hold you over until the proper show kicks off Saturday. This morning, Nintendo shared some updates related to the Pikmin franchise and has officially claimed November 1 as Pikmin Day, starting today and moving forward presumably forever.

Miyamoto also shared that the mobile game, Pikmin Bloom, is also getting a fairly substantial update soon with secret caves. In Bloom, players will be able to find maps that reveal caves that you can send your Pikmin into to battle and find treasure. You can also find maps for Bloom by playing Pikmin 4. Caves will be coming to Pikmin Bloom later this year.

The Pikmin Day presentation also reminded viewers that every Pikmin game is available on Switch and Switch 2, though no announcements or hints were made implying that Pikmin 1 and 2 would be coming to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service, which includes GameCube games on Switch 2. Those games can be purchased individually on the eShop.

Finally, Miyamoto brought actress Fuka Koshiba on the presentation (best known for voicing Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service) to share her appreciation for the Pikmin franchise (she likes to knit Pikmin hats that she shares on social media) and introduce a Pikmin short film. In the short, a Pikmin interacts with a toad, but I won’t spoil what happens. Miyamoto promised more shorts are on the way and in the future, they will be found in the Nintendo Today app.

Unfortunately, the stream concluded without a single reference to 2017's Hey! Pikmin. I wouldn't expect it to get a port to Switch 2 anytime soon.

The company wants to "capture institutional knowledge" before it's too late

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo of America is one of many companies investing in game preservation, and a new job listing gives us some insight into what those efforts look like. The company is looking to hire a "digital archivist" to build a library of historical material that can last for generations.

"We are seeking a Digital Archivist, Historical Systems to support the preservation, organization, and accessibility of historical hardware and software information," the company says in its job listing. "This role will design and implement a structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms."

That's a lot of technical words for a position that ultimately boils down to 'build an internal library.' A company like Nintendo of America may have vast piles of historical development documents, advertising materials, and software prototypes on hand, but if nobody knows where any individual thing can be located, it may as well be lost altogether.

While many players might hear the phrase "game preservation" and think of efforts to ensure games are playable on modern devices, the field is far broader than that. Organizations like the Video Game History Foundation specialize in preserving not individual games, but development documents and other historical ephemera providing context on how historical games were developed, released, and played in their time.

Game publishers are starting to invest in this area themselves. PlayStation has a vast vault of historical materials, and Blizzard is building the same sort of archive. For the most part, these archives are never intended to be viewed by the public, but their work can help developers looking to build on historical games. Archived materials might, for example, show up as bonus features in remastered games.

Nintendo's digital archivist "will establish standards and processes that ensure historical information remains discoverable, usable, and preserved for future generations." The company describes this as a 12-month contract position, so it's presumably hoping that its hire will set up an archive and workflow that employees can then add to autonomously.

Perhaps the most notable duty in the job listing is this: "Interview subject matter experts and long-tenured employees to capture institutional knowledge." Nintendo's made a point of hanging onto longtime staff even as other companies lay off developers with decades of experience, but even in an environment that values experience many of gaming's most notable developers are reaching retirement age. Saving their stories and experience for the next generation is going to be a massive boon.

There are games that come once in a decade and define an era for many. There’s a reason why we still talk about titles like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time or Grand Theft Auto V, for instance. Both games have made such an impact on the gaming community that they will be remembered forever.

The next game to get remembered for years to come is going to be Grand Theft Auto VI. It has already had such hype built up around it that no matter what happens on the release date, we will be talking about it for years.

Of course, there are several other reasons GTA VI will be remembered, whether it is the level of detail, the time put into it, or even the impact on the economy.

Grand Theft Auto V is remembered for its great story, the attention to detail, and many other things. Red Dead Redemption 2 is remembered for these as well. GTA VI will also be remembered for its attention to detail and how it revolutionized open world gaming.

The next Grand Theft Auto title is set to expand the map, increase the level of detail in NPCs, and showcase a level of attention never seen in a game before. If everything goes smoothly at launch, gamers will be talking about how it is the new standard for open world games.

Every game after this will feel like it doesn’t measure up to the detail of Rockstar’s latest project, and it will be used as the benchmark for nearly every other triple-A studio.

Rockstar's 38 new GTA 6 screenshots showcase incredibly detailed faces, Vice City's nightlife, and the gangs and scenes bringing Leonida to life.

One thing that gamers seem to always bring up is how long they waited for any particular game. We finally got a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and some of the first things people said was that they waited almost 30 years for it.

Kingdom Hearts players are the same way, as they often mention the wait between Kingdom Hearts 2 and Kingdom Hearts 3. Whenever there is a long wait for a sequel, we tend to latch onto it and bring it up in conversation.

With there being a significant wait of 13 years between GTA V and GTA VI, gamers are going to be talking about it for years to come, bringing it up like they had to wait in line for their favorite game for all those years or something.

Meme culture is powerful and stays around for a long time. For instance, the show King of the Hill stuck around thanks to meme culture. The same can be said for Skyrim, as it has many dedicated memes that have never gone out of style.

Odds are, there will be moments in GTA VI that get memed, whether it is the characters giving an odd look or one of the many wild NPCs. There are already memes using parts of the footage we have already seen, I can only imagine what will come from the game’s full release.

On top of this, the game has already generated the meme of “We got this before GTA VI.” This will evolve to GTA VII, and people will talk about how it used to be GTA VI.

Development studios are always trying to figure out when the best time to launch a game is. Typically, a studio wants to avoid launching a game at the same time as a competitor if the games are too similar. After all, they want to maximize their profits, so it only makes sense.

GTA VI had a massive impact on release schedules. Before anyone even knew the release date of GTA VI, companies were already trying to avoid being caught in the release window. Some were even trying to wait out giving a release date until GTA VI’s release date was announced.

Everyone knew the sway the game would have on the wallets of gamers, and they wanted to avoid potential losses. With this news hitting the mainstream, it will be remembered for a long time.

There’s often a conversation that people have when it comes to games and the consoles they are played on. It's all about what games are console sellers. This is typically reserved for games that are console exclusives, like Demon’s Souls for the PS5 or Gears of War E-Day for the Xbox Series X|S.

However, there has been a trend of people buying up consoles just so they can play GTA VI. They avoided buying a PS5 or an Xbox Series X|S until now just so they can play this game.

That is something that many people won’t forget. No matter if GTA VI is great or it flops, everyone who bought a console for it will remember the game for years to come. You don’t forget why you bought a console. I bought my PS5 specifically for Demon’s Souls.

Okay, GTA Online 2.0, or whatever they want to call it, isn’t going to last forever, but it will last for a long time. After all, GTA V Online has lasted for many years, and people are still playing it despite the game coming out in 2013.

Thanks to constant updates and a dedicated community, the online mode has stayed relevant for years. Now GTA VI Online will take the spotlight, and it will keep everyone’s attention after they finish the story.

Nobody knows when GTA VII will be released, and so GTA VI Online will be the go-to online mode for the Grand Theft Auto experience for possibly a decade or more. That will keep people talking for sure.

GTA Online 2.0 will be coming eventually, and there are some changes that Rockstar should make.

You may have heard it already. “GTA VI will cost the US economy $1 billion.” While that likely isn’t true, it is a game that will have a cultural impact, and there are estimates that state the US economy will take a hit to its productivity when it is released.

There is no telling how much money the economy could potentially lose on November 19th, but some businesses have already stated that they anticipate their workflow to slow down that day, and there are many who have already said they’re going to call out to play GTA VI.

Even if there is a small hit to the US economy, that will still be remembered for years. It will be a day that shows how many gamers became united by one game.

Let’s talk about sales numbers for a moment, because the gaming community remembers when a game does amazingly well and when it falls incredibly short. GTA VI is already doing amazingly well with pre-orders.

It is being estimated that pre-orders for GTA VI have already generated $751 million, and over 7 million units have been pre-ordered. That is a higher revenue than many other triple-A titles make, and that is also only on console, as the game won’t be on PC for a while.

It is estimated that GTA VI will generate over $1 billion in revenue for Rockstar, making it close to being one of the highest grossing games of all time. Give it a few years and sales of the game will most likely surpass even GTA V, which sold over 230 million copies. That is a number people will remember.

#4228. Gobs & Gears turns factory building into a goblin-powered demolition puzzle

The best advice Gobs & Gears gives you is to build it wrong. It may sound counterintuitive, but you lay out a route, rip it up the moment it’s done its job, and blow up the odd building along the way, all to finish a bomb for a goblin king who wants it immediately. It’s a logistics puzzler that’s out now on iPhone.

The map starts under a thick Fog. Just like London has been the past few days. You put up Scout Towers to burn it back in bursts, and each surge reveals lost Buildings that need to be brought back. For that, you need the right resources, which must be hauled around by Trundlers along conveyor routes you lay yourself. And if a mountain gets in your way, just blow it up.

Crafting runs from Rubble at the bottom to the Boom Core at the top, across sixteen resources, six tiers and 26 kinds of Building. Gobs from nearby Gob Camps can speed a building up or carry resources from places your routes haven’t reached yet. The maps are procedurally generated too, with roughly 281 quadrillion possible layouts.

Factory games like these make you live with your mistakes. A messy layout tends to stay messy. Gobs & Gear makes rebuilding the point. I’d say Mini Motorways is the nearest relative, where half the time you’re pulling up the road you placed five minutes ago.

There’s no grinding between runs and no punishing timers either. Given the Gob King’s mood, I thought there’d be a timer. It’s all pixel art, and the building names do a fair bit of the joking, the Smelty Hole and the Dig Pit among them.

Gobs & Gears is out today on iOS for a one-off $9.99 purchase.

If you’d prefer puzzles with fewer explosions, our list of the best strategy games on iOS is mostly bomb-free.

Opening their latest titles to fresh faces should lead to a big boost both in revenue and players, something they desperately need as they move onto their next project.

Relic is stacking up an easy win with the upcoming port of Company of Heroes 3, one of their stronger titles. Fans know the DLC song and dance and are far more willing to play ball, but Relic needs newcomers now more than ever.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. #4219. Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

Something you learn in 13 years of video game journalism is that some people react poorly to reading things they said. Being quoted can be scary. Now the words sound the way they did leaving your mouth, not the way they may have sounded inside your head.

Anyway, OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman recently complained that his remarks on a podcast, in which he bemoaned the inefficiencies of RAM sitting in personal PCs and not cooking away in AI data centers, were "taken out of context."

"From a global allocation perspective, actually it's quite terrible to have everyone have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and be used 5% of the time," he said. Later, Altman insisted, after quite some outcry, that "I actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers."

Clearly, one software developer took this as a challenge. Enter: Ram-Altman, "A bash script that emails Sam Altman once a day to report the RAM he missed."

Developed (and shared on GitHub) by self-described network operations manager Iain Kay, Ram-Altman is a simple script that automatically informs Altman, at his email, that you have RAM and you are not using it.

"There is RAM in your computer. Right now. Just sitting there, in a personal computer, being personal. You may have thought of this as 'a computer working normally.' On a recent episode of Cheeky Pint, the CEO of OpenAI offered another view," the tool blurb reads.

"So we wrote a script. If your machine has more than 10% of its RAM available, it sends one email a day to let Sam know. It seemed only fair. He can't fix the problem if nobody tells him where the RAM is."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

A sample message that might be sent to Altman, signed "a concerned RAM owner," reads: "Please don't be alarmed, but there is 8.6 GiB of RAM on my desk that isn't in a data centre. That's 56.2% of what's installed here, and as far as I can tell it has no plans today."

If you're wondering, the tool only looks at 10% unused RAM or greater because, "below that, your machine has suffered enough." If you need me, I'll be closing 47 browser tabs.

#4217. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4216. 8 Metroidvanias Where the World Feels Bigger the More You Learn About It

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

One of the best aspects of video games overall is how they allow people to learn about and explore enthralling worlds in fantasy, sci-fi, or historical settings.

Many gamers would choose to play third-person open-world or narrative-focused adventure titles to explore such worlds, but there are many other game genres that allow people to delve deeper into a world’s environments and lore, such as the backtracking-centered metroidvania.

While most metroidvania games are limited to a 2D side-scrolling-like perspective, many metroidvania games can feel just as large and expansive as those found in RPGs. Especially as players continue to travel through the titles' maps and learn more about their history and inhabitants.

DrinkBox Studios' Guacamelee! is a stylish Mexican folk art and lucha libre-inspired metroidvania that saw players travel throughout the lands of the living and the dead as agave farmer turned luchador Juan Aguacate.

However, DrinkBox strove to go bigger and better with Guacamelee’s sequel, Guacamelee! 2, as that game had Aguacate travel beyond his homeland into the Mexiverse, a multiverse full of wondrous and intriguing alternate timelines.

This game almost immediately made the universe of Guacamelee far larger and more complex than most players would have imagined by just playing the first game, with Guacamelee! 2 allowing Aguacate to meet alternate versions of friends and villains as well as entirely different realms such as El Otromundo.

Konami’s Castlevania franchise is full of titles that allow players to explore and learn more about the supernatural settings and subsequent entries, as they fight vampires and other monsters. One of the more accessible entries for new players would be Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

A third-person hack and slash metroidvania reboot of the series, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow has players embody the Brotherhood of Light knight Gabriel Belmont in 11th century Europe, as he sets out to defeat the titular Lords of Shadow and Satan himself.

However, Belmont quickly learns that there are far more dark powers hiding throughout the world as, in the Reverie and Resurrection DLCs, he travels to Carmilla's castle to defeat the ancient Forgotten One, only to become Dracula and menace humanity for hundreds of years.

From the best bosses to essential lore explanations, these are eight Metroidvanias that hide their best content behind the most unexpected paths.

Xbox consoles have become homes for many metroidvania titles over the years, with one of the earliest to debut exclusively on a Xbox console in an action-packed way being Chair Entertainment’s Shadow Complex.

Set in the same universe as Orson Scott Card's Empire book series, Shadow Complex is a military sci-fi metroidvania following Jason Fleming as he and his girlfriend, Claire, set out to explore some caves hidden in a mountain.

Things quickly go awry, though, as it’s revealed that the caves were an entrance to a labyrinth-like shadow complex run by the militant Progressive Restoration. Fleming is forced to explore the complex and steal the PR’s gear in order to rescue Clair and stop the PR from inciting a second civil war in the U.S.

One of the better metroidvanias to launch in 2026 was Drop Rate Studio’s Lovecraftian horror game DIVE or DIE - Children of Rain which takes place in the near future after most of the world was flooded by a supernatural, monster-making black rain.

Here, players must manage one of the last human settlements and routinely send people to dive into the leviathan and ruin-filled Abyssal Pool, in search of supplies and ways to appease the Cthulhu-like Rainmaker in 40 days before it destroys the world.

When players initially dive into the Abyssal Pool, they’ll first find the remains of skyscrapers and other buildings. As they continue to dive deeper and deeper below the surface, they’ll find that the Pool has almost no end in sight and is filled with all kinds of unspeakable horrors.

If you're looking for games that subvert your expectations, try these eight Metroidvanias that totally reinvent themselves halfway through.

As mentioned before, Xbox and Microsoft have supported and published many metroidvanias over the years, with some of the best they published undoubtedly being Moon Studios’ Ori and the Blind Forest and its sequel Ori and the Will of the Wisps.

The Blind Forest primarily takes places in the amazing Nibel Forest and its surrounding areas, but the first game teased other lands that were set to be explored in the Will of the Wisps.

Here, the cat-like spirit Ori and the owl Ku find themselves in the Niwen region, which has since suffered from the loss of its own Spirit Tree. This has resulted in Niwen’s inhabitants becoming corrupted and terrorizing each other, showcasing that the world of Ori is full of all kinds of magical forces and creatures.

Of all the Metroid games released over the years, the Metroid Prime subseries is arguably the most popular, with the series notably transitioning its sci-fi gameplay and maneuverability into first-person.

However, if players wanted to explore areas that feel bigger the more people learn about them, then there’s no better entry in the MP series to try out than Metroid Prime 2: Echoes.

Set roughly one year after the first MP, Metroid Prime 2: Echoes sees the bounty hunter Samus Aran travel to the planet Aether to rescue Galactic Federation Marines, only to discover that the planet is home to an advanced moth-like sentient race called the Luminoth and is at the center of a dimensional rift to an alternate hostile world called Dark Aether.

If you're looking for unexplored gems in video games, I recommend these ten Metroidvanias that are unexpected masterpieces.

Some of the more popular metroidvania series may feature vast, enthralling worlds, but sometimes metroidvanias created by small independent studios are those with the largest worlds, with one such game being Valdis Story: Abyssal City.

The second title created by Endlessfluff Games, Valdis Story: Abyssal City follows the fantasy sword-wielding warrior Wyatt and the mage Reina as they set out in search of Wyatt's father only to wind up in the sunken city of Sitheil.

From here, the two young heroes are forced to not only face off against endless waves of angels and demons but also explore and learn more about the seemingly ever-expanding Atlantis-like city of Sitheil, with the game’s ending even suggesting that other magical cities may be hidden throughout the world.

Without a doubt, the best metroidvania to play where the world feels bigger the more you learn about it is Team Cherry’s 2D masterpiece Hollow Knight.

Set primarily in the subterranean insectoid kingdom of Hallownest, Hollow Knight follows an unnamed horned Knight as they set out to explore a world that has since fallen into ruin following an outbreak of a mysterious, violence-inducing infection.

During the Knight’s travels, players will not only be able to interact with numerous insectoid inhabitants and learn more about Hallownest’s past, but also explore several subregions of the kingdom and learn about other far away lands and realms such as the City of Tears, Crystal Peak, and Dream Realm.

Looking for an exciting map to explore in the Metroidvania genre? We have the games with the best maps for you here.

#4215. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

#4214. Big Walk Ineligible For IGF Game Of The Year Due To AI Use

AI use in video games has never been a more hotly debated topic, and much like last year with Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, its masked use during development has impacted one of this year’s Game of the Year frontrunners, Big Walk. Turns out AI was used during Big Walk’s development, and it’s the game’s disqualification from the Independent Game Festival’s GOTY consideration that has led to that unfortunate discovery.

The IGF posted a statement (thanks, Aftermath) regarding its nominations this year, highlighting that some who vote for its GOTY nominees and award winners simply won’t consider games that used generative AI during their development. It seemed a fairly straightforward, somewhat expected stance. However, it became clear in the hours after that statement was posted that the reason IGF representatives were having such a tough time deliberating is because AI was used during Big Walk’s development.

As the BDS Boycott continues, Big Walk stands firm.

That revelation has led to Big Walk studio House House updating its FAQ to confirm that yes, AI was used during the game’s development process, and to explain how exactly it was implemented.

“In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs,” the new FAQ section reads.

LLM stands for large language model, AIs that are trained on vast amounts of text to help summarize, translate, and in some cases generate language.

“In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.”

The updated FAQ section continues, providing examples of when House House turned to AI during the latter stages of Big Walk’s development for help. It goes on to explain that a version of this was sent to IGF to clarify the studio’s use of AI, hence it being seemingly disqualified from GOTY consideration, and the matter becoming public knowledge.

House House then adds that the reason it didn’t disclose the use of AI during Big Walk’s development until now is because it isn’t mandatory on Steam, and that it is only disclosing the information now because “it’s a matter of public interest”. Letting your players know AI was used during development is arguably always a matter of public interest, not just when you get found out for not disclosing it in the first place, but it’s the arguably in that sentence that makes AI use in video games so divisive.

In the explanation’s penultimate paragraph, House House writes, "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'." Again, it might be argued that other studios see this and think quite the opposite, seeing Big Walk’s huge success and turning to AI also, and hiding it, since it worked for House House.

Big Walk will now not be considered for IGF’s GOTY award, and this could result in a knock-on effect where it fails to pick up nominations elsewhere. It has already been nominated for the Golden Joysticks GOTY, the winner of which will be announced this week. Even after winning, though, Big Walk might not be safe from having its win revoked. Expedition 33 lost its Indie Game Awards GOTY last year after AI use during development was unearthed after the GOTY had been awarded. The award was retroactively taken back and given to runner-up Blue Prince instead.

"I think most of the confusion boils down to context."
